characters: Senam: a curious seven-year-old Ghanaian girl with neat braided hair and green hair beads, wearing a yellow-and-brown check school dress and brown sandals.
Nana Dapaah: her warm elderly Ghanaian grandfather with short grey hair and beard, wearing an earth-toned cotton smock over dark trousers and holding a carved wooden walking stick.
Madam Boateng (class teacher): a smiling Ghanaian woman wearing a leafy-green patterned dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious girl’s voice for Senam; a calm, kind grandfather’s voice for Nana Dapaah
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and clear, with a pause for each test (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A gentle flute with light bird sounds (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The story follows the NaCCA Science content standards on living, non-living and once-living things (B1.1.1.2, B2.1.1.2). Stools, drums and mortars are often carved from wood in Ghana, so the example is familiar.
The story does not ask children to judge any belief about trees or spirits; it only describes what living things do.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the three groups (living, never alive, once alive) against the NaCCA Science B2 content standard B2.1.1.2.
Check that the explanation (grows, needs food and air, makes young ones) is right for the age.

teacherGuide.overview: A grandfather and a child sort things into living, never-alive and once-alive groups. It follows the NaCCA Science standard on living and non-living things (B2.1.1.2) and teaches the features of living things.
learningGoals: Name three things that living things do.
Sort objects into living, never alive and once alive.
Give one example for each group.
beforeReading: Ask: is a plant alive? Is a stone alive? Why?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and ask children to say the test for “alive”.
afterReading: Do a school walk and sort ten things into three groups.
Draw a chart: living, never alive, once alive.
discussion: Why do we not harm living things without a reason?
reflection: What living things do you see on the way to school?

support: Use picture cards and sort them in pairs.
stretch: Think of an object made from something once alive, such as paper, leather or cloth.

culturalNotes: The story follows the NaCCA Science content standards on living, non-living and once-living things (B1.1.1.2, B2.1.1.2). Stools, drums and mortars are often carved from wood in Ghana, so the example is familiar.
The story does not ask children to judge any belief about trees or spirits; it only describes what living things do.
localiseThis: Use trees, stones and wooden objects familiar to children.
Do not argue with children’s beliefs; focus on what living things do.
